title: Electrochemical Carbon Dioxide Reduction on Femtosecond Laser-Processed Copper Electrodes: Effect on the Liquid Products by Structuring and Doping
abstract: A femtosecond laser process is presented increasing the surface area of copper electrocatalysts for an electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR). The laser treatment allows us to tune the surface morphology and the chemical composition of the copper electrocatalysts. This tunability is used to correlate the role of the surface area and catalyst dopants with the selectivity of the CO2RR. The liquid products of the CO2RR are monitored through ex situ nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy. The products’ distribution shows that the electrode surface area plays a key role in the electrochemical conversion of CO2 into multicarbon liquid products. We show that sulfur dopants boost the production of formate. Remarkably, by co-doping sulfur and fluoride, we show that the chalcogenide dopant counteracts the known boosting effect of fluoride to convert CO2 into multicarbon products. Oxygen doping in the range of 2−19 atom % does not significantly affect the distribution of liquid products from CO2 electroreduction. In a broad perspective, this work highlights the potential of the femtosecond laser process to fine-tune surfaces to produce photoand electrocatalyst materials.

sections.text: KEYWORDS: femtosecond laser, material processing, electrochemical hydrogenation, carbon dioxide, copper, sulfur, liquid products

sections.heading: 1. INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
Decarbonization of society is critical to mitigating the impact of our growing population on the Earth’s climate, which is recognized in several of the United Nations’ goals for sustainable development.1,2 One appealing way to reduce humanity’s carbon footprint is by capturing and converting carbon dioxide, the most important greenhouse gas, into valuable fuels or chemical commodities. Electrochemical hydrogenation of carbon dioxide (i.e., CO2 reduction reaction, CO2RR) is an excellent way to carry out such valorization in a renewable way. Cathodic CO2RR uses hydrogen from water and renewable electricity (derived from, e.g., solar, wind, or hydropower) to produce industrially valuable chemicals,3−7 with the potential to be coupled with the anodic valorization of biomass to minimize the number of byproducts generated.8
Operational costs (OPEX) account for ca. 90% of the total production cost for the CO2RR, 9 and the catalyst’s stability
and electricity usage are critical factors affecting the OPEX costs. For CO2RR to be feasible for large-scale implementation, the electrocatalysts should be efficient, stable, and scalable. Copper-based materials are the most promising CO2RR electrocatalysts, the only ones reported to date that are able to drive electrochemical carbon−carbon coupling to convert CO2 into multicarbon products.
10 The economic feasibility of CO2RR depends on the actual value of the electrochemically generated products;9,11,12 therefore, reaction selectivity is of

pivotal importance. There is an enormous interest to convert CO2 into oxygenate compounds that are liquid under normal conditions of pressure and temperature (e.g., formic acid, ethanol, n-propanol). The liquid nature facilitates transport and storage, and the oxygenate compounds could be directly fed into existing combustion engines to smooth the transition from fossil to renewable fuels for transportation and other purposes.13−18 The parameters driving the CO2RR selectivity toward formation of multicarbon products are still a matter of debate. Some of the different hypotheses to explain the selectivity of nanostructured copper toward multicarbon products are (1) enhancement in (100) sites that could geometrically favor the carbon−carbon coupling,19−23 (2) high density of grain boundaries on the nanostructured catalyst,13,14,24,25 (3) increases in the interfacial pH due to high currents on highly roughened surfaces,26−29 (4) moderate interfacial CO2 concentration,
30,31 and (5) residual (subsurface) oxygen that could increase the coverage of CO, facilitating C−C coupling.15,32−35 Besides the effect of oxygen doping of copper on the CO2RR selectivity toward formation of multicarbon products, sulfur doping has also been shown to significantly affect the selectivity. Sulfur content in copper favors the reaction toward generation of formate/formic acid.36−39
This work aims at shedding light on the role of surface roughness and surface doping in the selectivity of electrochemical CO2 electroreduction to liquid oxygenate products (ethanol, n-propanol, and formic acid). To assess the role of these parameters, we structure copper electrodes through femtosecond laser (fs-laser) irradiation.40,41 Laser-induced surface structures can be tuned from tens of nanometer to 100 μm.40 The enhanced surface structures have been proved beneficial in electrocatalytic reactions, especially in electrolysis technologies.42−47 Although it is an ablation process, elements from the femtosecond laser process environment are incorporated.47,48 Therefore, additional features are enabled, such as hyperdoping49,50 or an increased catalytic activity due to further added catalyst elements,47 thus allowing us to assess the role of dopants on the CO2RR selectivity.

sections.heading: 2. EXPERIMENTAL SECTION
sections.text:
2.1. Cu-Based Electrocatalyst Preparation. The electrocatalysts were prepared from polycrystalline copper foils (Alfa Aesar Puratronic, 99.998% metal basis, 0.5 mm thickness). Prior to measurements or nanostructuring procedures, the copper foils were electropolished for 3 min in 85 wt % H3PO4 by applying 2 V vs. a carbon counter electrode. Structured copper was prepared by laser ablation using a Spitfire titanium-sapphire (Ti:Sa)-based regenerative amplifier from Spectra Physics and a Mantis seed laser from Coherent. The ablation process was performed in a similar manner as previously reported,43 using laser pulses at a wavelength of 800 nm with a 60 fs duration. The beam was focused into the process chamber with a lens of 500 mm of the effective focal distance. The laser spot was measured to have ca. 80 μm diameter (measured as intensity 1/e2). To structure the copper samples, they were scanned meandering with a constant line pitch of 30 μm. The level of ablation was tuned to generate electrocatalysts either with a high surface area (strongly structured copper) or with a medium surface area (moderately structured copper). Strongly structured copper (sCu) was obtained by two ablation scans, using a laser fluence of 5.57 J/cm2 with a repetition rate of 10 kHz and a linear scan velocity of 4 mm/s, corresponding to ca. 2 × 310 pulses per area spot on the surface. Moderately structured copper (mCu) was prepared by one ablation scan, using a laser fluence of 3.58 J/cm2, with a repetition rate of 1.25 kHz and a linear scan velocity of 37.5 mm/s, corresponding to less than 3 pulses per
area spot on the surface. The ablation process was performed in a chamber filled with three different gases, Ar, O2, and SF6, respectively. The gases were continuously fed to the process chamber reaching a pressure inside the chamber of ca. 800 mbar (corresponding to the partial pressure of the fed gas). Therefore, six different copper-based electrocatalysts were prepared as depicted in Table 1. After the laser
process, the samples were thoroughly cleaned by sonication in deionized water, acetone, 2-propanol, and again with deionized water (2 min sonication in each solvent).
2.2. Physical Material Characterization. The samples were characterized by (ex situ) scanning electron microscopy (SEM), using a setup from Zeiss (EVO 50, MA10). The surface analysis of the chemical content was performed by energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) using a Bruker Nano QUANTAX 800 system with an XFlash-6 detector. EDX spectra were measured with an acceleration voltage of 5 kV at a magnification of 500, integrating an area of about 150 × 200 μm2. Additional measurements were performed at 10 and 15 kV to measure the composition of the sample as a function of depth. The EDX analysis was focused on the elements present in the processing gases, namely, sulfur, fluorine, argon, and oxygen. Carbon was measured within the same range for all samples. In general, it is detected naturally on each sample without seamless preservation of high-purity handling and due to the formation of byproducts during the electrochemical treatment. A representative raw data set of the used EDX-data acquisition is shown in Figure S1.
2.3. Electrochemical Characterization and Product Analysis. The experiments were performed in a custom two-compartment cell made of polycarbonate, similar to the one described in the report of Kuhl et al.6 The two compartments were separated by an anion exchange membrane (Selemion AMV, ACG Inc.). Prior to the electrochemical experiment, 10 mL of 0.1 M KHCO3 (Sigma-Aldrich, 99.99% trace metal basis) was filled into the working electrode compartment and 11 mL was filled into the counter electrode compartment. The electrolyte was then saturated for ca. 15 min with CO2 (purity grade 5.5) at a flow rate of 20 sccm. The gas was kept bubbling at 20 sccm during data acquisition. The electrochemical data was acquired using a Bio-Logic VSP potentiostat in a three-electrode configuration setup. A platinum foil was used as the counter electrode, and a reversible hydrogen electrode was used as the reference electrode. All electrode potentials in this work are reported with respect to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) potential reference scale. The electroreduction experiments were performed by potentiostatic electrolysis for 1 h. The applied electrode potential was corrected to compensate 85% of the electrolyte resistance (the last 15% was compensated after the experiment to avoid instability in the potentiostat control). The electrolyte resistance was estimated by the real component of the impedance at high frequency. The frequency was chosen by performing constant potential impedance spectroscopy.6 The electrochemically active surface area (ECSA) and the roughness factor (RF) were estimated from pseudocapacitance measurements, which were performed before and after the electrolysis experiments.51 The roughness factor (RF) was calculated as

sections.heading: 3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
sections.text:
3.1. Surface Morphology. The strongly structured samples processed in Ar are shown in the top-view SEM image in Figure 1a. The laser-treated copper samples have conical spikelike structures regularly distributed along the surface. The spikes have >50 μm interspike separation and heights in the same range. The spikes are covered with a cauliflower-like porous substructure consisting of round nanoparticles, as can be seen in the high-magnification SEM
image of Figure 1b. A cross-sectional view is presented in Figure S3. The samples processed in O2 feature comblike structures (see Figure 1c), covered with similar cauliflower-like porous substructures as those observed for the copper samples prepared in Ar. These features are depicted in the highmagnification top-view SEM image of Figure 1d and the crosssectional view in Figure S4. Structuring the copper samples in the presence of SF6 gas during the laser process results in comblike structures, as shown in Figure 1e. The highmagnification top-view SEM image (see Figure 1f) and the cross-sectional view show a layerlike porous substructure rather than the cauliflower-like substructure observed for the samples prepared in Ar or O2. The hierarchical structures of the lasertreated copper samples resemble the cauliflower pattern previously reported for laser-structured copper surfaces.52
Similar nanostructured surfaces have been previously generated by treating copper with O2 plasma 35 and have been
https://doi.org/10.1021/acsaem.1c00759 ACS Appl. Energy Mater. 2021, 4, 5927−5934
5929
shown to boost the catalytic activity for the electrochemical conversion of CO2 into C2+ hydrocarbons. In these studies, the authors correlate the enhancement of the C2+ selectivity with a significant amount of surface oxygen, reaching the highest current efficiency toward ethanol production for samples containing 24% of surface oxygen. While the gas present in the chamber during the laser process has a significant influence on the surface morphology of the strongly structured samples, it does not significantly influence the morphology of the medium-structured samples. Top-view SEM images of the medium-structured samples prepared in Ar, O2, or SF6 are displayed in Figure S6a−f, and the similarities show a negligible influence of the gas on the morphology of the medium-structured samples. 3.2. Pseudocapacitance Surface Roughness Factor. The electrochemically active surface estimated by pseudocapacitance measurements is listed in Table 2 along with the
surface composition of sulfur, fluorine, and oxygen. The highest roughness factor (RF = 124) is measured for the sCuSF6 samples. Although the SEM images in Figure 1 appear similar or even less rough than the other strongly structured samples, the value is almost twice as high as for the samples
laser-processed under O2, for example. This RF value indicates a higher porosity of the samples structured under SF6. In comparison, the samples processed in Ar and O2 have RF values of 75 and 62, respectively.
3.3. Energy-Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy Analysis. The chemical surface analysis also differs for the samples due to the different preparation methods and the applied background gases. The lowest trace gas concentration is found for the laser-structured samples processed in Ar. The Ar content is below the detection limit of about 0.1 atom % for EDX analysis for the mCu-Ar and the sCu-Ar samples. These samples feature an oxygen content of about 2−6 atom %, which is within the natural range for copper samples, that comes into contact with ambient air. This is consistent with the polished copper reference. In contrast, significant amounts of background gas elements are incorporated during the structuring of copper under SF6. The sample sCu-SF6 measures sulfur content in a range of about 2.5 up to 5.0 atom %, fluorine up to 25 atom %, and oxygen of about 22.2 atom %. The sample mCu-SF6 features a lower sulfur content of about 1.2 atom %, 1.4 atom % fluorine, and 18.1 atom % oxygen. Since the sulfur and fluorine contents remain stable even after occasional heating to about 80 °C during sporadic measurements over a long period of 6 months, it is concluded that the elements are permanently bound in the copper matrix. However, after the electrochemical treatment at any potential, the sulfur and fluorine contents are reduced for the sCu-SF6 sample to about 1 atom % each. This is in accordance with Shinagawa et al.36 where sulfur is incorporated up to a content of 62 atom % and only a measurable amount remained in the Cu matrix after the electrochemical treatment. They stated that the range of the sulfur content is negligible for the selectivity effect. The extent to which these contents reduce toward zero during prolonged electrochemical treatment, or whether it is a stable value, remains to be investigated in the future. Although sCu-O2 and mCu-O2 samples are processed in O2, the oxygen content is 18.5 and 10.1 atom %, respectively, and lower than those of the corresponding samples processed under SF6. An explanation for this is the higher roughness factor of the SF6 samples, indicating an enhanced porosity and corresponding

formation of the native oxide over the large surface area. Consequently, a higher oxygen content within the electron− matter interaction volume during the EDX analysis is detected. By comparison, the oxygen content in similar studies is up to more than 30%.33,35,36
Note on the Element Depth Profile. We also find a decreasing element concentration of the background trace gases when the acceleration voltage for the EDX measurement is increased from 5 to 10 and 15 kV. As expected, when parts of the ablation plume are resolidified on the surface, this indicates that the amount of the incorporated elements increases with increasing proximity to the surface in the order of the electron’s penetration depth. An example of the depth profile of molybdenum in a nickel matrix is given in ref 48. Furthermore, we observed that fluorine and oxygen are incorporated deeper into the surface than sulfur because the EDX signal decreases continuously at 10 and 15 kV. On the contrary, sulfur is only detected close to the detection limit of 0.1 atom % at acceleration voltages higher than 5 kV. 3.4. Liquid Product Analysis. The current efficiency of the liquid products generated during the electrochemical CO2 reduction experiments is displayed in Figure 2 for different samples and at different electrochemical potentials. Formate is the main liquid product of CO2 electroreduction at −0.7 V. However, at this potential, the strongly roughened samples (i.e., sCu-Ar and sCu-O2) also produce C2+ alcohols (npropanol and ethanol) with total current efficiency in the range of 7−9%. As the applied potential becomes more negative, all samples start producing C2+ alcohols, with the current efficiency being proportional to the sample′s roughness. For all measurements, the current efficiency for the electrochemical CO2 reduction into acetate, allyl alcohol, and methanol is below 1%. Therefore, these products are not considered in our discussion. The current efficiency vs the potentials is also shown as a scatter plot in Figure S7. It is worth noticing that the strongly structured samples with the highest sulfur and fluorine contents (sCu-SF6) mainly produce formate as a liquid product irrespective of the applied electrode potential. Only at the highest electrode potential considered (i.e., −1.0 V) were
minor amounts of n-propanol and ethanol detected (current efficiency even less than the values measured on polished polycrystalline copper). The lack of selectivity of the sCu-SF6 sample with more than 25 atom % F on its surface (as indicated in Table 2) toward C2+ alcohols is unexpected. Fluorine has been reported to significantly boost the selectivity of CO2 electroreduction on copper toward ethylene and ethanol.53 We assigned sulfur on the surface of sCu-SF6 as the inhibitor for the C2+ pathway of CO2 electroreduction. The highly roughened samples produced in the presence of Ar and O2 gases have similar current efficiencies toward C2+ alcohol production (see Figure 2), even though these samples have a ca. three-fold difference in surface oxygen content. This similarity suggests that for oxygen contents above 2 atom %, oxygen doping does not significantly affect the selectivity of CO2 reduction into multicarbon compounds. The current efficiency trends observed in this study differ from the report on plasma-activated copper samples, where samples with ca. 30% surface oxygen content show the highest selectivity for conversion of CO2 into C2+ alcohols.
15 This divergence is related to differences in the sample morphology, as the plasma-activated samples consist of cubelike clusters forming crystal (100) sites, while the samples in this work are clusters of round nanoparticles without distinct orientation sites. The role of sulfur in the electrocatalytic conversion of CO2 into formate is still a matter of debate. It has been hypothesized that the chalcogenide dopant could stabilize the *OCHO intermediate species, leading to partial-to-complete deactivation of the CO pathway toward C2+ products. 36 Alternatively, it has been proposed that the sulfur dopant could completely change the CO2 electroreduction catalytic pathway by activating the water in the hydration shell of the metal cations in the double layer. The activated water could dissociate to form adsorbed Hads species that can react with adsorbed CO2 molecules (i.e., surface acid−base reaction) to produce HCOO* intermediates that would be the promoter of formate.38 Except for the sulfur-containing samples, all of the structured samples with a higher surface roughness feature a higher current efficiency for the CO2 reduction to C2+ alcohols,
https://doi.org/10.1021/acsaem.1c00759 ACS Appl. Energy Mater. 2021, 4, 5927−5934
5931
namely, n-propanol and ethanol, at less-negative electrode potentials. The current efficiency is in the range of 7−15% and it is electrode potential-dependent. The strongly roughened samples produce C2+ alcohols at −0.7 V electrode potential (Figure 3, top row), while the smoother samples do not produce significant amounts of C2+ alcohols. The efficiency toward the C2+ alcohols on the strongly roughened copper reaches a maximum at −0.9 V. This effect is magnified for the highly structured samples and it is correlated to the depletion of CO2 in the interfacial area due to the higher currents that develop as the potential becomes more negative. It has been shown that in a H-type electrochemical cell filled with 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte, the interfacial concentration of CO2 tends to zero when the current density approaches 25 mA/cm2.5454 For our high-surface-area CO2-reduction electrocatalysts, this limit in current density is reached in the potential region of −0.9 to −1.0 V vs RHE and we estimate this limit to occur rather in the range of about 20 mA/cm2 (see Table S1). Even if the laser-processed copper samples have different morphologies depending on the treatment conditions, they all consist of clusters of round nanoparticles, which are not expected to lead to any significant enhancement of (100) sites. However, the samples show an enhancement in the current efficiency for the CO2 reduction to C2+ products, with the current efficiency being dependent on the sample’s roughness factor (see Figure 3). This enhancement indicates that the surface roughness is a critical parameter to boost the current efficiency toward the formation of C2+ products. The enhancing effect could either be in the sense of a high density of grain boundaries or high interfacial pH due to the high hydrogen evolution reaction. It is important to notice that current efficiency toward C2+ alcohols of high-surface-area copper does not significantly depend on the gas present in the chamber during the laser treatment.

sections.heading: 4. CONCLUSIONS
sections.text:
We prepared structured copper electrodes for the CO2RR by a femtosecond laser using different background gases. By tuning the laser-treatment conditions, the electrode surface area and the dopants (i.e., O, S, F) on the electrocatalyst surface are controlled. We exploited this tunability to correlate the effect of the electrode roughness factor and catalyst dopants with the selectivity of the electrochemical CO2 conversion into liquid products. The results show that sulfur incorporation inhibits production of C2+ molecules, and formate ions are the only liquid product detected. Remarkably, these results on SF6modified samples show that the inhibiting role of sulfur over C2+ products counteracts the expected boosting effect of fluorine dopants. We also showed that an oxygen surface composition in the wide range of 2−19 atom % does not significantly affect the selectivity of CO2 electroreduction into C2+ liquid products. It is also shown that the electrode surface area plays a pivotal role in the selectivity of the electrochemical conversion of CO2 into C2+ liquid products. This work presents a novel route to produce nanostructured surfaces with a controlled roughness and different dopants. Such control over the surface could be exploited for the rational design of catalysts for photo- and electrocatalytic reactions.
